Here's my attempt

> A patient was admitted to the intensive care unit with an acute exacerbation of chronic heart failure.

Exacerbation: his heart failure got suddenly worse

> His medical history included heart failure with an ejection fraction of 20% bioprosthetic aortic-valve replacement for bicuspid aortic stenosis,

His heart only pumped out 20% of the blood in it with each beat, a normal ejection fraction is over 55%. They replaced of his valves because it wasn't letting enough blood thru

> endovascular stenting of an aortic aneurysm, and placement of a permanent pacemaker for complete heart block.

His aorta (the bodies biggest artery which comes directly off the heart) was bulging so they basically put a tube inside of it and sewed to try to get to heal to normal size (I feel like that was confusing. Sorry) his heart had electrical issues so they put in a pacemaker

> An Impella ventricular assist device was placed for management of acute heart failure, and a continuous heparin infusion was initiated for systemic anticoagulation.

They fed a tube up thru his artery into his heart and temporarily installed a tiny pump to help get blood thru. They also pumped an IV blood thinner to prevent blood clots (being immobile in a hospital and also having foreign shit in your vascular system increase risk of blood clots)

> During the next week, the patient had episodes of small-volume hemoptysis, increasing respiratory distress, and increasing use of supplemental oxygen (up to 20 liters delivered through a high-flow nasal cannula).

He was coughing up blood and had troublebreathing. 20 liters per minute is a LOT of o2. Patients are normally on 2-5ish, obviously depending on condition

> During an extreme bout of coughing, the patient spontaneously expectorated an intact cast of the right bronchial tree.

He coughed up a cast of the airways of his right lung. They didn't specify what the cast was but I'm thinking his lung filled up with blood which then clotted and he coughed it up. When a pt is in heart failure the blood can't go thru easily so it backs up into the blood vessels of the lungs and can get forced into the airway

> The right bronchial tree consists of three segmental branches in the upper lobe (blue arrows), two segmental branches in the middle lobe (white arrows), and five segmental branches in the lower lobe (black arrows). The patient’s trachea was subsequently intubated, and flexible bronchoscopy revealed a small amount of blood in the basilar branches of the right lower lobe.

They put a tube down his throat and then shoved a camera in it, the camera found blood in the bottom of his right lung

> The patient was extubated 2 days later and had no further episodes of hemoptysis. One week after extubation, he died from complications of heart failure (volume overload and poor cardiac output) despite placement of the ventricular assist device.

They took the tube out 2 days later and he didn't cough up anymore blood.  He died from having too much fluid volume and his heart not pumping well enough

>*Dialogue Options*: This feature was one of the best new aspects of a major western title and is a great innovation to open world games. I have no doubt the developer will continue to implement and improve on it. Perhaps adding more options or greater freedom and opportunities.

Its definitely a great aspect and one that a major city-based crime game should implement, But i dont see it as an innovation to open world games.

>*Overall Depth and Quality of Life*: By far the greatest strength of the western title is it’s sheer amount of detail and the sheer scope of the world. Seeing this amount of depth in a city-based crime game could drastically change the style of the game and perhaps give the series a new direction. However i doubt it would be as deliberately slow paced as the western title.

I think adding dialogue options and fleshing out npcs would do wonders for the depth of the game but a big part of the western title's depth is hunting and crafting which obviously doesnt fit with the city game

>*The Gang System*: Arguably the main pillar of the western title’s story, the gang act as a driving force for the story and are basically fully developed NPC’s in the world which makes it feel like they actually exist. For a city-based crime game. a gang system who clearly work on many levels however my wish would be that its not so tied up with every aspect of the game generally speaking. The obvious change for me would be making our character the leader of the gang and introducing a tonne of mechanics to maintain and grow your criminal enterprise.


>*Periodic Setting*: Technically this isn’t a gameplay element but more of just the premise of the game. I’m obviously preaching to the choir when i say that the city game would benefit ALOT from setting a game in the 70’s or 80’s. Not only is it the best time to cash in on nostalgia, but it would also give the game an overall vibe and aesthetic which would be crafted by the developer. Plus. don’t even get me started on the soundtrack possibilities.


A previous city game was set in the 80s and was super great, another periodic game would be dope.
>*Combat*: The western title’s combat brought some great improvements such as gore/dismemberment and physics but overall it was really lacking. I know that everything in this game is purposefully slow but in a western game i don’t think it translates very well at times. However when it works, it works beautifully. Declared dead? That's not how it works. Organs are collected from patients who are brain dead and considered unlikely to ever recover but are anatomically alive.

Also even if you are an organ donor they still need permission from your family. Plus keeping you alive is better for organ donation. Ive only Ever known of organs collected from patients who are brain dead but anatomically "alive".

Not true. I'm a nurse, I don't work in the operating room but I have a general idea of how the organ collection process works. The wheels are all put in motion when the person is alive but their brain is damaged enough that there's considered no likelihood of them returning to consciousness. When someone is in this position (on life support) we, as nurses call the organ donation network who then comes in and speaks with the family about organ donation. Once the family gives consent, the organ recovery surgery is performed on the anatomically and legally still living patient. 

Someone isn't declared dead when their brain stops working but when their heart stops.
